title: LOTO 101: Control of Hazardous Energy
description: A 5-minute microlearning on OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147: the energy types, who does what, the seven steps of lockout/tagout, group lockout, and safe restart. Ends with a 10-question knowledge check.

blocks.title: Why lockout/tagout matters

image.alt: A maintenance technician in a bump cap, hairnet, and safety glasses beside a stopped food-plant conveyor, attaching a red padlock and danger tag to its electrical disconnect. Hands are away from the belt and all moving parts.

blocks.script: Every machine in this plant stores energy. When someone reaches into a machine that starts up unexpectedly, the result is amputations, crushing injuries, and deaths. OSHA's lockout/tagout standard, 29 CFR 1910.147, exists to stop that. OSHA estimates that following it prevents about 120 deaths and 50,000 injuries every year. In the next five minutes you'll learn how to make a machine safe before you work on it, and keep it safe until you're done.

beats.text: OSHA estimate: ≈120 deaths and 50,000 injuries prevented each year

blocks.title: Hazardous energy comes in many forms

image.alt: An industrial machine area showing an electrical disconnect, hydraulic hoses, a pneumatic air line, and a steam pipe.

blocks.script: Hazardous energy is any energy that can move, heat, or hurt. Electrical energy in motors and panels. Mechanical energy in belts, blades, and flywheels that keep spinning. Hydraulic and pneumatic energy trapped under pressure in hoses and cylinders. Thermal energy and steam. Chemicals and gas in lines. And gravity, which can drop a raised part on you. Most machines have more than one. Your placard lists every source, and every one must be controlled.

beats.text: Control every source on the placard

blocks.prompt: Match each energy source to the device that isolates it.

pairs.answer: Air valve with lockout and bleed
Gate valve with valve cover lock

blocks.title: Authorized and affected employees

image.alt: A maintenance worker in a bump cap, hairnet, and safety glasses applying a red padlock and danger tag to a disconnect while a line operator in a hairnet and white smock watches from a safe distance.

blocks.script: An authorized employee locks out a machine and services it. Only trained, authorized employees apply locks. An affected employee runs the machine or works in the area. They must recognize a lockout and never restart locked-out equipment. If your job means reaching in, like clearing a jam or cleaning, you must be trained as authorized and lock out first. Everyone else must respect every lock and tag.

beats.text: Affected: runs the machine or works nearby
Reaching in to clear a jam or clean? Lock out first
Everyone respects every lock and tag

blocks.title: Prepare, notify, shut down

image.alt: A technician reading a laminated lockout placard mounted beside a packaging machine.

blocks.script: Step one: prepare. Read the machine's lockout placard so you know every energy source and where its isolation point is. Step two: notify the affected employees that you are shutting the machine down and locking it out. Step three: shut the machine down using its normal stop control, never by pulling a disconnect while it's running under load.

beats.text: 3 · Shut down with the normal stop

blocks.title: Isolate, then lock and tag

image.alt: Close-up of a gloved hand closing a red personal safety padlock and danger tag onto an electrical disconnect handle in the off position.

blocks.script: Step four: isolate. Move every energy-isolating device to the safe position: open the disconnect, close the valves. A control-panel stop button is not an isolation point. Step five: apply your own lock and tag to every isolation point. One person, one lock, one key. Your key stays with you. Use a tag alone only where your written procedure says a lock can't be applied, and then with extra protection.

beats.text: A stop button is NOT isolation
5 · Your lock + tag on every point
One person · one lock · one key

blocks.prompt: Tap every true energy-isolation point on this machine. Leave the others.

image.alt: A mixer station with an emergency stop button, a lockable electrical disconnect, a pneumatic ball valve, and an operator touchscreen.

blocks.title: Release stored energy, then verify

image.alt: A technician in a bump cap, hairnet, and safety glasses pressing the start button on a stopped machine, standing clear of all moving parts, with a red padlock and danger tag visible on the nearby disconnect. Guards are in place.

blocks.script: Step six: release or restrain stored energy. Bleed air and hydraulic pressure, block raised parts, let flywheels stop, and let hot parts cool. Step seven: verify. Make sure everyone is clear, then try to start the machine. Nothing should happen. If the procedure calls for a voltage test, a qualified electrician does it. Then return the controls to off. Only now is the machine at zero energy and safe to work on.

beats.text: 7 · Verify: everyone clear, try to start
Controls back to OFF → zero energy

blocks.prompt: Put the seven lockout steps in the right order.

items.label: Shut down with the normal stop

blocks.title: A locked machine can still hurt you
blocks.body: Hydraulic cylinders, springs, flywheels, capacitors, raised forks and hot surfaces keep their energy after the disconnect is off. Release or block it, then verify, every time.

blocks.title: Group lockout and shift change

image.alt: A group lockout box covered in several workers' padlocks hanging on a plant wall.

blocks.script: When a crew works on the same machine, use group lockout. One authorized employee locks out the machine, verifies zero energy, and puts the keys in a group lockbox. Then every worker adds their own personal lock to the box. No one is protected by someone else's lock. At shift change, the incoming worker applies their lock before the outgoing worker removes theirs, so the machine is never left unprotected.

beats.text: Every worker adds their own lock
Never rely on someone else's lock
Shift change: lock on before lock off

blocks.stem: You arrive to help a coworker clear a jam. Their lock is already on the disconnect and they say, "You're covered, I locked it out." What do you do?

choices.label: Apply my own lock and tag, and verify zero energy, before I reach in.
choices.feedback: Right. Your lock is the only lock that protects you. They could finish, remove theirs, and restart while you're still inside.

choices.label: Start working. Their lock is on, so the machine can't start.
choices.feedback: Their lock protects them, not you. If they remove it while you're inside, nothing stops a restart.

choices.label: Hang my own danger tag next to their lock.
choices.feedback: A tag is a warning, not a physical barrier. Where a lock can be applied, apply your lock.

blocks.title: Removal, restart, and the rules that never bend

image.alt: A technician removing their own padlock from a disconnect after the work area has been cleared, with the guard reinstalled.

blocks.script: When the work is done, remove tools and put the guards back. Make sure everyone is clear. Then each person removes only their own lock. If a lock is left behind, only a supervisor may remove it, following plant rules. Before restart, tell the affected employees the locks are off. Never work on a machine that isn't locked out, even for a quick job. If unsure, stop and ask. Now let's check what you know.

beats.text: No shortcuts · if unsure, stop and ask

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of lockout/tagout?
questions.explanation: LOTO prevents the unexpected start-up or release of stored energy while people service equipment.

answers.text: To prevent unexpected start-up or release of energy while equipment is serviced
To keep production running during maintenance
To record who last used a machine
To stop unauthorized people from operating machines during breaks

questions.prompt: Who is allowed to apply a lockout device?
questions.explanation: Only trained, authorized employees apply locks. Affected employees recognize lockouts but don't apply them.

answers.text: A trained authorized employee
Any affected employee who operates the machine
Whoever is closest to the disconnect
Only the plant manager

questions.prompt: Pressing the machine's emergency stop button is enough to isolate its energy.
questions.explanation: Stop buttons and control circuits are not energy-isolating devices. Isolate at the disconnect, valve, or block.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Select every energy source you must control on a machine that has a motor, an air cylinder, and a raised platen.
questions.explanation: The motor is electrical, the air cylinder is pneumatic, and a raised platen stores gravitational energy.

answers.text: Electrical
Pneumatic
Gravity
Steam (there is no steam line on this machine)

questions.prompt: What comes immediately after you apply your lock and tag?
questions.explanation: After locking and tagging, release or restrain stored energy, then verify.

answers.text: Release or block stored energy
Start the repair
Notify affected employees
Remove the guard

questions.prompt: How do you verify a machine is at zero energy?
questions.explanation: With everyone clear, attempt a start (a qualified person does any voltage test the procedure requires), then return controls to off.

answers.text: Clear everyone, try to start it, then return controls to off
Look at the lock to confirm it is closed
Ask the operator if it is off
Wait five minutes

questions.prompt: Your coworker's lock is already on the disconnect. Are you protected?
questions.explanation: Each worker must apply their own lock. Someone else's lock protects them, not you.

answers.text: No. I must apply my own lock and tag
Yes. One lock is enough for the crew
Yes, if I can see them
Only if the job takes less than 10 minutes

questions.prompt: During a shift change on a locked-out machine, what is the correct order?
questions.explanation: Protection must be continuous: incoming workers apply their locks before outgoing workers remove theirs, following your plant's shift-change procedure.

answers.text: The incoming worker locks on before the outgoing worker removes their lock
The outgoing worker removes their lock, then the incoming worker locks on
The supervisor removes all locks and re-applies one
The machine is restarted and locked out again

questions.prompt: Select every action required before restarting after the work is done.
questions.explanation: Clear tools, reinstall guards, confirm everyone is clear, notify affected employees, and each person removes only their own lock.

answers.text: Remove tools and reinstall guards
Confirm everyone is clear and notify affected employees
Each person removes only their own lock
Remove any lock left by a coworker who went home

questions.prompt: A tag may replace a lock whenever a lock is inconvenient.
questions.explanation: A tag alone is used only where the written procedure says a device can't accept a lock, and then with additional protective measures.

answers.text: True
False

image_prompt_rules: Every person wears a hairnet (beard net if facial hair), safety glasses, and no jewelry; bump caps, not hard hats. Locks only on disconnects or valves, never on stop buttons or panels. No readable text on tags or signs. Photorealistic, clean modern food-production plant, stainless steel equipment.
